title: Ethical Practice in Sensitive Research — NPE, Trauma & Living People

subChunks.title: Ethical Practice in Sensitive Research — NPE, Trauma & Living People

storyBeats.txt: Genealogy is, at its deepest level, a form of historiography — the reconstruction of lives. And those lives belong to people. To their descendants. To communities. When the research is about the living, or about events within living memory, the ethical dimensions multiply.

The professional codes we follow give us principles. But principles require judgment to apply. No code can tell you exactly how to handle the moment when a client's DNA results reveal that her late father was not her biological father. Or when a researcher discovers that their family hero was also a colonial administrator responsible for forced displacement.
This lesson is about cultivating that judgment — the capacity for ethical reasoning that goes beyond compliance to genuine wisdom.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Professional ethics in genealogy are often discussed in terms of rules and codes — the APG Code of Ethics, GDPR requirements, professional indemnity obligations. These are essential, but they are the floor of ethical practice, not the ceiling. The genuinely difficult ethical questions arise not when the rules are clear but when they are silent or in conflict: when client interests and third-party interests diverge; when a discovery could help one person while harming another; when historical truth conflicts with living family narratives.

Sensitive research — involving NPEs, adoptee searches, trauma histories, living people — requires not just compliance with professional codes but the development of ethical judgment: the ability to reason through genuinely difficult situations, weigh competing interests, and reach decisions that can be justified to all parties affected.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Privacy of Living People

The genealogical principle that living people must be protected is nearly universal across professional codes. The practical application: do not publish identifying information about living individuals without consent; do not share data about living people with third parties; do not include living people in public online family trees without their explicit agreement; treat any information about living people's health, relationships, or circumstances as confidential.

Particular care is required for: children (never publish identifying information about living minors); living biological relatives identified through DNA (they did not consent to being identified through your client's research); living people identified through forensic genealogy (the genealogist's role ends at identification — contact is a law enforcement decision).

NPE Research: Multiple Stakeholders

A non-paternity event discovery affects at minimum: the client who discovered it; the client's documented parent (who may be living and unaware); the biological parent (who may not know they have a biological child); and the biological parent's family (who did not consent to exposure). In some cases it affects siblings, extended family, and generations of descendants.

Professional obligations: the genealogist's primary duty is to the commissioning client. However, that duty does not extend to actively harming third parties. The professional response to an NPE discovery: inform the client of the finding factually; allow the client to determine what to do with the information; do not contact third parties without the client's explicit instruction; provide referrals to support organisations; and be honest about the emotional impact of potential disclosures on multiple family members.

Trauma and Historical Research

Historical genealogical research frequently encounters trauma: slavery, genocide, forced migration, family separation, abuse. Research into these areas requires: awareness that the researcher's own emotional response to the material is legitimate and should be managed; awareness that descendants of affected communities have their own relationship to the history that differs from the researcher's; and the ability to present findings in a way that is historically honest without being gratuitously distressing.

For researchers working with African American genealogy across the 1870 wall, Indigenous genealogy including residential school records, or Holocaust-era Jewish genealogy, there is a specific responsibility to engage with the community's established scholarship and frameworks rather than approaching the material purely as a technical puzzle. The community's own historians and genealogists have developed methodological and ethical approaches that should inform and shape the researcher's work.

Intergenerational Trauma and DNA Discovery

DNA discoveries can reactivate intergenerational trauma: an adoptee who discovers they are the product of sexual violence; a descendant of enslaved people who identifies their enslaver through DNA; a Holocaust survivor's grandchild who discovers murdered relatives through the Yad Vashem database. These are genealogical research findings that carry profound psychological weight.

The professional genealogist's role: to provide accurate information; to do so sensitively; to refer to specialist support where appropriate; and to allow the client to determine the pace and extent of disclosure at their own pace. It is not the genealogist's role to manage the client's emotional process — but it is their responsibility not to be reckless with information that could cause serious harm.

Research Into Difficult Family Histories

Clients may commission research that reveals morally uncomfortable facts about their own families: ancestors who were perpetrators of violence, colonial abuses, or other historical wrongs. This requires the genealogist to: present findings factually without editorialising; resist the pressure (sometimes explicitly applied by clients) to minimise, explain away, or exclude uncomfortable findings; and be honest about what the evidence shows regardless of how it reflects on the family.

The genealogical record is not sanitised. Ancestors are fully human — capable of both virtuous and harmful acts. A family history that presents only the flattering facts is not a history; it is a mythology. The professional genealogist's commitment to evidence-based conclusions extends to uncomfortable evidence as well as comfortable evidence.

Consent in Genealogical Research

Genealogical research about living people requires their consent. In practice this means: interviewing family members requires their consent to use what they share; photographing private family documents requires the document owner's consent; publishing living people's information in any form requires explicit consent. The fact that information has been shared informally in a family context does not constitute consent to use it in a published or publicly shared family history.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why a genealogist has ethical responsibilities not just to the client who is paying them, but also to the other living people their research might affect.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: You are researching the family history of a client, Robert, who wants a full family history narrative. In the course of your research, you discover that Robert's great-grandfather was a colonial administrator in British India who, based on documented archival evidence, participated in decisions that led to significant civilian casualties during a famine in the late 19th century. Robert did not ask about this and has expressed pride in his family's imperial service history. How do you handle this finding in your report?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
This is a genuine ethical tension between: (a) honesty and the genealogist's commitment to evidence-based findings; (b) sensitivity to a client who has expressed pride in his family's history; and (c) the broader responsibility to historical truth.

The finding must be included in the report. It is documented, evidenced, and relevant to the family history being constructed. Omitting it would be a selective presentation that creates a mythologised rather than historical account. The genealogist's professional obligation is to follow the evidence wherever it leads, including to findings the client may find uncomfortable.

How to include it: present the finding factually and in its historical context — explaining the documented administrative role, the documented decisions, and the historical record of the famine and its causes. Avoid moral editorialising (do not describe the great-grandfather as 'evil' or 'heroic'). Present the historical scholarship on the relevant famine so the client understands the historiographical context, not just the individual facts about his ancestor. Note any mitigating context that the evidence supports — but do not introduce context that has no evidential basis merely to soften the finding.

Before delivering the report: it is good practice to contact the client to say that the research has uncovered some historically difficult material, and to check whether he wants to receive it as part of the main narrative or in a separate section. This respects his autonomy while being honest about the content. Do not suppress the finding — but give the client the opportunity to prepare for it.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: You are a genealogist who has been conducting research for a client into her biological family. You have identified, through DNA, that she has a half-brother — a man in his 50s whose Ancestry profile shows a large family and whose public tree does not include any children from outside his marriage. Your client wants to make contact. However, you notice that the half-brother's profile has been inactive for three years and his public tree has not been updated. What ethical considerations apply to your advice to your client about how to approach contact?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Multiple ethical considerations apply: (1) The half-brother's right to privacy — he may not know about your client's existence; his wife and children almost certainly do not. Contact risks revealing an NPE to his family without his prior consent or knowledge. (2) The risk of harm to his family relationships — this is not a trivial consideration; disclosure could have serious personal consequences for him and people who did not choose to be involved. (3) Your client's right to know her biological family — genuine and important. (4) The inactive profile — the three-year inactivity may indicate he has withdrawn from genealogical research, is unwell, or has died. Sending a contact request to an inactive account creates uncertainty about who might read it and when.

Advice to your client: (1) Do not contact him through Ancestry messaging, since the account appears inactive and there is no certainty about who reads it. (2) Consider an intermediary approach — organisations like DNA Detectives' contact facilitation services, or writing a carefully worded letter to an address you may have found through documentary research. A letter allows him to process the information privately before deciding whether to respond. (3) Be prepared for all possible responses: denial, enthusiasm, request for time, no response. None of these responses invalidates the DNA evidence, but all of them are legitimate reactions. (4) Engage with a specialist support organisation (NORCAP, DNA Surprises community) before making contact, to think through how to frame the initial communication. (5) Be clear in your own mind that your role as genealogist ended at identification — the contact decision and its consequences are entirely your client's to manage.
learningObjectives: Apply the principle of living-people privacy protection to specific scenarios involving DNA discovery and published family histories.
Describe the multiple stakeholders affected by an NPE discovery and the genealogist's obligations to each.
Explain why genealogical research into traumatic historical events requires engagement with affected community frameworks.
Demonstrate ethical reasoning about uncomfortable historical findings — the obligation to include them honestly while presenting them sensitively.
commonMistakes: Contacting biological relatives identified through a client's DNA without explicit instruction from the client — a serious breach of ethical and professional boundaries.
Omitting uncomfortable historical findings from a family history narrative to avoid distressing the client — this produces mythology, not history.
Failing to distinguish between the genealogist's role (providing accurate information) and a counsellor's role (managing emotional responses) in NPE and trauma scenarios.
Assuming that because a family member shared information informally, it can be included in a published family history without separate consent.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies all affected stakeholders in an NPE or sensitive discovery scenario.
Demonstrates principled reasoning that balances client interests with third-party welfare, using professional ethics frameworks.
Shows commitment to including uncomfortable historical findings while presenting them in their proper historical context.
Maintains clear professional boundaries — the genealogist's role versus the counsellor's, the researcher's role versus the contact facilitator's.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The transmission of psychological trauma from one generation to the next through family dynamics, cultural transmission, or epigenetic mechanisms; relevant to genealogical research involving slavery, genocide, and forced displacement.
Online peer support community for people who have experienced unexpected genealogical DNA discoveries — NPEs, unknown half-siblings, donor conception; an important referral resource for genealogists.
UK organisations specialising in facilitated contact between adoptees and biological family members; provide intermediary services that reduce the risk of direct, unexpected contact.

The clearly defined limit of the genealogist's role — providing accurate information and research — beyond which the client's decisions, emotional processes, and relationships are entirely their own responsibility.

questions.questionHtml: Why must a professional genealogist never include identifying information about living people in a publicly shared family history without their consent?
options: Living people cannot be historical subjects — family histories cover only deceased individuals
Living people's privacy rights are protected under data protection legislation and ethical codes; their consent is required before their information is disclosed publicly
It is a violation of copyright to publish information about living people
Online family tree platforms prohibit the inclusion of living people
questions.correctAnswer: Living people's privacy rights are protected under data protection legislation and ethical codes; their consent is required before their information is disclosed publicly
questions.explanationHtml: GDPR, the APG Code of Ethics, and all major genealogical professional standards require that identifying information about living people not be published without their consent. Living people retain privacy rights over their personal information — including their inclusion in a family history narrative or online tree.

questions.questionHtml: You discover that your client's great-great-grandfather was convicted of a serious crime in 1895. Your client has not asked about legal records and the family has no knowledge of this. How should you handle this finding?
options: Omit it from the report — your client didn't ask for criminal records and may be distressed
Include it factually in the relevant section of the report, in its historical context, as part of the comprehensive family history — omitting relevant evidence would produce a misleading account
Mention it verbally but not include it in the written report
Only include it if the client explicitly requests criminal records
questions.correctAnswer: Include it factually in the relevant section of the report, in its historical context, as part of the comprehensive family history — omitting relevant evidence would produce a misleading account
questions.explanationHtml: A comprehensive family history follows the evidence wherever it leads. Selectively omitting uncomfortable facts produces a mythology rather than a history. The finding should be presented factually, in its historical context (criminal justice of the period; social circumstances), without moral editorialising — the same standard applied to any other finding.

questions.questionHtml: A client whose DNA research revealed an NPE is now severely distressed and beginning to rely on you for daily emotional support. She calls you multiple times a week to discuss her feelings about the discovery. What is the ethically and professionally appropriate response?
options: Provide the emotional support — it is part of the service and you are the only one who understands her situation

Acknowledge her distress empathetically, explain clearly that your role is as a genealogical researcher not an emotional support provider, and refer her to appropriate professional support (a therapist, a specialist DNA discovery support group) while continuing to provide the genealogical information she needs
End the professional relationship immediately since the client's emotional needs have exceeded your scope
Ask the client to manage her emotional responses on her own time and only contact you for genealogical questions
questions.correctAnswer: Acknowledge her distress empathetically, explain clearly that your role is as a genealogical researcher not an emotional support provider, and refer her to appropriate professional support (a therapist, a specialist DNA discovery support group) while continuing to provide the genealogical information she needs
questions.explanationHtml: Professional genealogists are not therapists. Providing ongoing emotional support beyond the genealogist's competence and role is harmful to both the client (who needs professional therapeutic support, not a genealogist) and the researcher (who may provide inadequate support and damage their own professional boundaries). The appropriate response maintains professional empathy while redirecting to appropriate specialist services.
